ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All procedures and materials were approved by an institutional review board prior to the recruitment of participants.
Participants were sixth and seventh grade students enrolled in one of three middle schools in and around a medium-sized city in the Southeastern United States.

All students at the schools were eligible to participate if they were enrolled in the sixth grade during the 2008-2009 school year, enrolled in the seventh grade during the 2009-2010 school year, and were not in selfcontained homeroom classes.
On average, participants were 11.32 years old (SD = 0.63, Missing: 8) at the time of the first survey.
Across the study period, 520 participants completed the full battery of questionnaires at Timepoint 1, 474 at Timepoint 2, 428 at Timepoint 3, and 406 at Timepoint 4.
Students were recruited as part of the larger efforts of the project.
When parental consent and student assent were obtained, participants were scheduled to complete the assessment at the participating middle schools.
Participants were compensated with a $10 USD Walmart gift card for their participation in the survey.
Participants were instructed that these questions referred to the participant and their friends, as compared to the broader peer network in classrooms.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: In line with our pre-registered analysis plan, we attempted to conduct a sensitivity power analysis using the powRICLPM package for R (Mulder, 2023) to identify the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) with 80% power for the cross-lagged effects and the random intercept correlations (see Giner-Sorolla et al., 2024). Unfortunately, due to the mathematical constraints which arose from the models' high intraclass correlations and moderate random intercept correlations, formal MDES calculations using this package were not feasible. These constraints reflect the mathematical incompatibility between high between-person variance and the additional complexity of cross-lagged parameters, resulting in non-positive definite covariance matrices in the power simulation framework. This is a limitation of the package's utility for sensitivity power analysis.

It is unclear if null results for within-person effects are due to a lack of power or the absence of a true effect. With that in mind, all conclusions regarding within-person cross-lagged effects should be viewed cautiously until an agreed-upon process for conducting sensitivity analyses for RI-CLPMs emerges. The effect sizes reported here can be used to guide future a priori power analyses, an area where the powRICLPM package demonstrates excellent utility. Regarding the between-person associations between random intercepts, a sensitivity analysis using the pwr package for R (Champely, 2020) indicated we can detect correlations as small as |r| = 0.18 with 90% power at = .05 with 𝛼 N = 304 (i.e., the smallest number of cases for any variable across all waves).

table.title: Longitudinal Associations Between Perceived Peer Reactions and Aggressive Behaviors
table.research_questions:
1. What is the relationship between one's expectations of their friends' reactions to negative behaviors (e.g., cheering on a fight) and physical aggression?
2. What is the relationship between one's expectations of their friends' reactions to negative behaviors (e.g., cheering on a fight) and relational aggression?
3. What is the relationship between one's expectations of their friends' reactions to positive behaviors (e.g., initiating teacher intervention) and physical aggression?
4. What is the relationship between one's expectations of their friends' reactions to positive behaviors (e.g., initiating teacher intervention) and relational aggression? Research Question 1
1. Within-participants, relatively greater expectations for friends' support for negative behaviors at one timepoint will predict relatively greater physical aggression at the subsequent timepoint.
2. Within-participants, relatively greater physical aggression at one timepoint will predict relatively greater expectations for friends' support of negative behaviors at the subsequent timepoint.
3. Children who generally expect their friends to be more supportive of negative behaviors will report greater physical aggression.

Research Question 2
4. Within-participants, relatively greater expectations for their friends' support of negative behaviors at one timepoint will predict relatively greater relational aggression at the subsequent timepoint.
5. Within-participants, relatively greater relational aggression at one timepoint will predict relatively greater expectations for their friends' support of negative behaviors at the subsequent timepoint.
6. Children who generally expect their friends to be more supportive of negative behaviors will report greater relational aggression.

Research Question 3
7. Within-participants, relatively greater expectations for their friends' support of positive behaviors at one timepoint will predict relatively lower physical aggression at the subsequent timepoint.
8. Within-participants, relatively lower physical aggression at one timepoint will predict relatively greater expectations for their friends' support of positive behaviors at the subsequent timepoint.
9. Children who generally expect their friends to be more supportive of positive behaviors will report lower physical aggression.

Research Question 4
10. Within-participants, relatively greater expectations for their friends' support of positive behaviors at one timepoint will predict relatively lower relational aggression at the subsequent timepoint.
11. Within-participants, relatively lower relational aggression at one timepoint will predict relatively greater expectations for their friends' support of positive behaviors at the subsequent timepoint.
12. Children who generally expect their friends to be more supportive of positive behaviors will report lower relational aggression.
table.datasets_used: This data is drawn from the Inclusive Violence Prevention Project (IVP; Sullivan et al., 2009). This study involved data collection from sixth and seventh grade student from two urban middle schools and a semi-rural middle school in the Southeastern United States. Participants completed measures at the beginning and end of the sixth and seventh grades (Wave 1: August 2008; Wave 2: May 2009; Wave 3: August 2009; Wave 4: May 2010). The urban schools served a predominantly Black student population (83-85%). The semi-rural was located in a rural setting within a close proximity to the urban area (i.e., "Rural Fringe" by the Census Bureau). This school served a more diverse student population.
table.data_availability: The dataset is not publicly available
table.access_date: Data will be accessed after this pre-registration has been posted.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants were recruited as part of the larger IVP project. Students in all non-self-contained homerooms were approach individually or in small groups to introduce the project and review assent and consent forms. Middle schoolers and their parents received copies of the consent forms that included contact information for study staff and the Office of Research Subjects' Protection at the home institution of the original researcher. Students received a $5 gift card for showing the consent form to their parents and returning it to research staff, regardless of the decision to participate. Once active parental consent and student assent were obtained, student were scheduled to complete assessments at the participating middle schools. Students received $10 for their participation in the survey.

All self-report measures were collected using a Computer Aided Personal Interview (CAPI). Questions were displayed virtually while students listened to audio recordings of each question through headphones worn by the participants. Students independently responded to questions using a mouse or trackpad. Research assistants were available to assist participants who had questions or experienced difficulties. Students who chose not to participate in the study were asked to leave the room.
table.measured_variables:
Expectations of Peer Reactions

Participants completed a measure of their perceptions about how their friends would feel about their possible behaviors in a given scenario. Participants answered questions about six scenarios. Each scenario involved the participant imagining a social context (e.g., "You see two kids your age about ready to start a fight in school."). Participants then answered two questions about how they thought their friends would react if they enacted a specific behavior for each scenario. One question involved a negative behavior (e.g., "What would your friends think if you cheered on the fight?"). The other question involved a positive behavior (e.g., "What would your friends think if you went to get a teacher?"). Participants selected whether they thought their friend would support the behavior, not support the behavior, or would be neutral about the behavior. Participants also had the option to skip each question.

Answers will be recoded such that the neutral option will be coded as 0, the support option will be coded as +1, and the unsupportive option will be coded as -1. For each time point, the mean of responses for each subscale will be specified as the independent variables. 

Physical and relational aggression were measured with the Problem Behavior Frequency Scale (PBFS). Participants indicated how often the did a given action (e.g., "Picked on someone", "Shoved or pushed someone") in the last 30 days using a numerical scale (1 = Never, 2 = 1-2 times, 3 = 3-5 times, 4 = 6-9 times, 5 = 10-19 times, 6 = 20 or more times). Participants had the option to skip each question (coded as 7). We will recode skipped items to 0. For each time point, the mean of responses for each subscale will be specified as the dependent variable. Importantly we will only use the items which Farrell et al. (2018) included in the psychometric assessment of the PBFS. Please see file "AggressionItems_RICLPM.pdf" for the specific item language.

---References---
Farrell, A. D., thompson, E. L., Mehari, K. R., Sullivan, T. N., & Goncy, E. A. (2018). Assessment of in-person and cyber aggression and victimization, substance use, and delinquent behavior during early adolescence. Assessment, 27(6), 1213-1229.
table.statistical_outliers: Rather than remove or Winsorize reponses, extreme scores will be retained for analysis.
table.prior_knowledge: WTB and EB have no prior knowledge of this dataset beyond what has been reported in previous theses, dissertations, and peer-reviewed articles. To our knowledge, the expectations of peer reactions items from this dataset have not been used elsewhere.
table.statistical_tests:
Model Specification
To test our hypotheses, we will use random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al., 2015) using lavaan (Rosseel et al., 2025) syntax for R (see Mulder & Hamaker, 2021). We plan to specify a model which includes expectations of friends' reactions to both positive and negative behaviors as independent predictors. Physical and relational aggression perpetration will be specified as the dependent variable in separate models. If the variance inflation factor (VIF) of the specified model is greater than five (i.e., the multicollinearity between the predictor variables is potentially problematic; Kim, 2019), we will specify separate models for each predictor (Alin, 2010). Please see file "RCode.R" for planned code.

Covariates
Each model will include covariates to account for group differences based on school. These will be included as time-invariant covariates which will be used to predict the random intercepts for the independent and dependent variables in the model. As students were drawn from three schools, we plan to include two (i.e., k-1) dummy coded covariates with one school as an arbitrary reference group.

---References---
Alin, A. (2010). Multicollinearity. Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews: Computational Statistics, 2(3), 370-374.
 
Hamaker, E. L., Kuiper, R. M., & Grasman, R. P. P. P. (2015). A critique of the cross-lagged panel model. Psychological Methods, 20, 102-116.

Kim, J. (2019). Multicollinearity and misleading statistical results. Korean Journal of Anesthesiology, 72(6), 558-569.   

Mulder, J. D., & Hamaker, E. L. (2021). Three extensions of the random intercept cross-lagged panel model. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 28(4), 638-438. 

Rosseel, Y., Jorgensen, T., & De Wilde, L. (2025). lavaan: Latent Variable Analysis. doi:10.32614/CRAN.package.lavaan, R package version 0.6-20, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=lavaan.
table.statistical_power: We refrain from simulating a dataset with expected effect sizes due to the nascent stage of this line of inquiry. We will conduct and report a sensitivity power analysis using the powRICLPM package for R. As this requires specifying the model, we refrain from conducting this power analysis prior to our pre-registration since the data has already been collected. We will use this package to determine the smallest effects we can detect with at least 80% power.
table.inference_criteria:
Prior to making inferences, we will assess model fit criteria. We will proceed if the model displays at least acceptable fit: a chi-squared test which is not statistically significant (p greater than .050), RMSEA less than .08, TLI greater than .90, SRMR less than .08, CFI greater than .90. We recognize that qualifying a model as displaying acceptable fit is nuanced. We will look at all fit indices holistically to determine our final judgement about the model's fit and report this flexibility in any manuscripts.

Hypotheses will be supported if the standardized regression coefficient for the hypothesized pathway is in the predicted direction and associated with a computed p-value less than .050.
table.assumption_violation_model_non_convergen: If the multicollinearity assumption is violated (i.e., VIF greater than 5), we will run separate models for each predictor rather than combining them into one model.
table.exploratory_analyses: Any analysis conducted beyond our pre-registered hypothesis tests will be deemed exploratory.

Participants completed measures at the beginning and end of the sixth and seventh grades (Wave 1: August 2008; Wave 2: May 2009; Wave 3: August 2009; Wave 4: May 2010). The urban schools served a predominantly Black student population (83-85%). The semi-rural was located in a rural setting within a close proximity to the urban area (i.e., "Rural Fringe" by the Census Bureau). This school served a more diverse student population.
table.data_availability: The dataset is not publicly available
table.access_date: Data will be accessed after this pre-registration has been posted.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants were recruited as part of the larger IVP project. Students in all non-self-contained homerooms were approach individually or in small groups to introduce the project and review assent and consent forms. Middle schoolers and their parents received copies of the consent forms that included contact information for study staff and the Office of Research Subjects' Protection at the home institution of the original researcher. Students received a $5 gift card for showing the consent form to their parents and returning it to research staff, regardless of the decision to participate. Once active parental consent and student assent were obtained, student were scheduled to complete assessments at the participating middle schools. Students received $10 for their participation in the survey.

All self-report measures were collected using a Computer Aided Personal Interview (CAPI). Questions were displayed virtually while students listened to audio recordings of each question through headphones worn by the participants. Students independently responded to questions using a mouse or trackpad. Research assistants were available to assist participants who had questions or experienced difficulties. Students who chose not to participate in the study were asked to leave the room.
table.measured_variables:
Expectations of Peer Reactions

Participants completed a measure of their perceptions about how their friends would feel about their possible behaviors in a given scenario. Participants answered questions about six scenarios. Each scenario involved the participant imagining a social context (e.g., "You see two kids your age about ready to start a fight in school."). Participants then answered two questions about how they thought their friends would react if they enacted a specific behavior for each scenario. One question involved a negative behavior (e.g., "What would your friends think if you cheered on the fight?"). The other question involved a positive behavior (e.g., "What would your friends think if you went to get a teacher?"). Participants selected whether they thought their friend would support the behavior, not support the behavior, or would be neutral about the behavior. Participants also had the option to skip each question.

Answers will be recoded such that the neutral option will be coded as 0, the support option will be coded as +1, and the unsupportive option will be coded as -1. For each time point, the mean of responses for each subscale will be specified as the independent variables. 

Physical and relational aggression were measured with the Problem Behavior Frequency Scale (PBFS). Participants indicated how often the did a given action (e.g., "Picked on someone", "Shoved or pushed someone") in the last 30 days using a numerical scale (1 = Never, 2 = 1-2 times, 3 = 3-5 times, 4 = 6-9 times, 5 = 10-19 times, 6 = 20 or more times). Participants had the option to skip each question (coded as 7). We will recode skipped items to 0. For each time point, the mean of responses for each subscale will be specified as the dependent variable. Importantly we will only use the items which Farrell et al. (2018) included in the psychometric assessment of the PBFS. Please see file "AggressionItems_RICLPM.pdf" for the specific item language.

---References---
Farrell, A. D., thompson, E. L., Mehari, K. R., Sullivan, T. N., & Goncy, E. A. (2018). Assessment of in-person and cyber aggression and victimization, substance use, and delinquent behavior during early adolescence. Assessment, 27(6), 1213-1229.

table.statistical_tests:
Model Specification
To test our hypotheses, we will use random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al., 2015) using lavaan (Rosseel et al., 2025) syntax for R (see Mulder & Hamaker, 2021). We plan to specify a model which includes expectations of friends' reactions to both positive and negative behaviors as independent predictors. Physical and relational aggression perpetration will be specified as the dependent variable in separate models. If the variance inflation factor (VIF) of the specified model is greater than five (i.e., the multicollinearity between the predictor variables is potentially problematic; Kim, 2019), we will specify separate models for each predictor (Alin, 2010). Please see file "RCode.R" for planned code.

Covariates
Each model will include covariates to account for group differences based on school. These will be included as time-invariant covariates which will be used to predict the random intercepts for the independent and dependent variables in the model. As students were drawn from three schools, we plan to include two (i.e., k-1) dummy coded covariates with one school as an arbitrary reference group.

table.statistical_power: We refrain from simulating a dataset with expected effect sizes due to the nascent stage of this line of inquiry. We will conduct and report a sensitivity power analysis using the powRICLPM package for R. As this requires specifying the model, we refrain from conducting this power analysis prior to our pre-registration since the data has already been collected. We will use this package to determine the smallest effects we can detect with at least 80% power.
table.inference_criteria:
Prior to making inferences, we will assess model fit criteria. We will proceed if the model displays at least acceptable fit: a chi-squared test which is not statistically significant (p greater than .050), RMSEA less than .08, TLI greater than .90, SRMR less than .08, CFI greater than .90. We recognize that qualifying a model as displaying acceptable fit is nuanced. We will look at all fit indices holistically to determine our final judgement about the model's fit and report this flexibility in any manuscripts.

Hypotheses will be supported if the standardized regression coefficient for the hypothesized pathway is in the predicted direction and associated with a computed p-value less than .050.
table.assumption_violation_model_non_convergen: If the multicollinearity assumption is violated (i.e., VIF greater than 5), we will run separate models for each predictor rather than combining them into one model.
table.exploratory_analyses: Any analysis conducted beyond our pre-registered hypothesis tests will be deemed exploratory.

Peer norms are linked to aggressive behaviors -attempts to harm someone who does not wish to be harmed (Allen & Anderson, 2017) -during adolescence as both a promotive and constraining factor.
text.formatted: Peer norms are linked to aggressive behaviors -attempts to harm someone who does not wish to be harmed <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allen & Anderson, 2017)</ref> -during adolescence as both a promotive and constraining factor.

text.text: Adolescents may prefer friends over non-friends as sources of social information (Slagter et al., 2023) and may engage in aggressive or nonviolent behaviors as a means of peer acceptance (Laursen et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Adolescents may prefer friends over non-friends as sources of social information <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Slagter et al., 2023)</ref> and may engage in aggressive or nonviolent behaviors as a means of peer acceptance <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Laursen et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Recent evidence suggests adolescent behavior is shaped by friendship influence in addition to normative pressure (Zingora & Flache, 2025).
text.formatted: Recent evidence suggests adolescent behavior is shaped by friendship influence in addition to normative pressure <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Zingora & Flache, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Less is known, though, about the role of intrapersonal expectations of peer reactions to aggressive and nonviolent conflict resolution strategies.
We examine longitudinal associations between youths' expectations of friends' reactions to these strategies and youths' aggressive behavior perpetration among middle schoolers.
Social norms regulate behavior by communicating what is typical and acceptable within a social context.

Norms can be classified as either descriptive (i.e., perceptions of others' common behaviors) or injunctive (i.e., perceptions of the social approval or disapproval of behaviors; Cialdini et al., 1990).
text.formatted: Norms can be classified as either descriptive (i.e., perceptions of others' common behaviors) or injunctive (i.e., perceptions of the social approval or disapproval of behaviors; <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Cialdini et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: While both types guide behavior, injunctive norms may be particularly informative for aggressive behaviors that carry social evaluative weight (Cialdini & Trost, 1998).
text.formatted: While both types guide behavior, injunctive norms may be particularly informative for aggressive behaviors that carry social evaluative weight <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cialdini & Trost, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: When individuals perceive that others would disapprove of aggression, they may be less likely to enact it; if aggression is perceived as socially sanctioned, they may be more likely to perpetrate it (Henry et al., 2000).
text.formatted: When individuals perceive that others would disapprove of aggression, they may be less likely to enact it; if aggression is perceived as socially sanctioned, they may be more likely to perpetrate it <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Henry et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Understanding how early adolescents perceive norms around aggression -and whose approval informs these behaviors -is critical as peer influence intensifies.

Early adolescence (i.e., roughly ages 10 -14) is a period with heightened susceptibility to peer influence (Steinberg & Monahan, 2007), as youth reorient from caregivers to peers as primary sources of social influence and behavioral guidance (Brown & Larson, 2009).
text.formatted: Early adolescence (i.e., roughly ages 10 -14) is a period with heightened susceptibility to peer influence <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Steinberg & Monahan, 2007)</ref>, as youth reorient from caregivers to peers as primary sources of social influence and behavioral guidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brown & Larson, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Before this shift, friends are not yet salient evaluative referents whose anticipated reactions inform decision-making (e.g., Larson & Richards, 1991), so meta-perceptions of friends' reactions may be less construct-relevant.
text.formatted: Before this shift, friends are not yet salient evaluative referents whose anticipated reactions inform decision-making (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Larson & Richards, 1991)</ref>, so meta-perceptions of friends' reactions may be less construct-relevant.

text.text: Peer relationships also become central to identity formation, and social acceptance is prioritized (Brechwald & Prinstein, 2011), shaping middle schoolers' attunement to peer norms.
text.formatted: Peer relationships also become central to identity formation, and social acceptance is prioritized <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brechwald & Prinstein, 2011)</ref>, shaping middle schoolers' attunement to peer norms.

text.text: Perceived peer norms supporting aggression predict aggressive behavior among youth: adolescents who perceive aggression as normative responses within their peer contexts, through both descriptive and injunctive norms, are more likely to perpetrate it (Henry et al., 2000; Salmivalli & Voeten, 2004).
text.formatted: Perceived peer norms supporting aggression predict aggressive behavior among youth: adolescents who perceive aggression as normative responses within their peer contexts, through both descriptive and injunctive norms, are more likely to perpetrate it <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Henry et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Salmivalli & Voeten, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The normative context may vary by type of aggression.

Physical aggression (i.e., direct physical harm to others) is typically counter-normative, particularly in middle school when youth internalize prohibitions against physical violence (Coie & Dodge, 1998), and early adolescents typically perceive it as disapproved by peers (Xie et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Physical aggression (i.e., direct physical harm to others) is typically counter-normative, particularly in middle school when youth internalize prohibitions against physical violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Coie & Dodge, 1998)</ref>, and early adolescents typically perceive it as disapproved by peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Xie et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, relational aggression (i.e., behaviors which harm others through damage to relationships or social status) occupies more ambiguous territory and may be perceived as more normative (Crick et al., 1999).
text.formatted: In contrast, relational aggression (i.e., behaviors which harm others through damage to relationships or social status) occupies more ambiguous territory and may be perceived as more normative <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Crick et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analytic evidence suggests that early adolescents who perpetrate relational aggression may maintain, or even enhance, their social status in middle school (Casper et al., 2020), implying that peer groups may tolerate or approve of it (Rose et al., 2004; Vaillancourt & Hymel, 2006).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic evidence suggests that early adolescents who perpetrate relational aggression may maintain, or even enhance, their social status in middle school <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Casper et al., 2020)</ref>, implying that peer groups may tolerate or approve of it <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Rose et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Vaillancourt & Hymel, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Most of this literature, though, reflects generalized peer norms, which may be too broad to capture relevant influences on aggression.

During early adolescence, when close friendships are forming and intensifying, youth may be less concerned with what peers in general think and focus more on what their friends think (Rubin et al., 2006).
text.formatted: During early adolescence, when close friendships are forming and intensifying, youth may be less concerned with what peers in general think and focus more on what their friends think <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Rubin et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Examining expectations about how specific close others (i.e., friends) would respond to their behaviors therefore requires moving beyond general peer norms.
Such expectations are meta-perceptions (Kenny, 1994).
text.formatted: Such expectations are meta-perceptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kenny, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-perceptions refer to individuals' beliefs about how others perceive them (Kenny & DePaulo, 1993).
text.formatted: Meta-perceptions refer to individuals' beliefs about how others perceive them <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Kenny & DePaulo, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike general normative beliefs about what behaviors are approved or disapproved, meta-perceptions involve expectations about how particular relationship partners view or would evaluate the self.
Their study has foundations in symbolic interactionist theory, which posits that individuals come to evaluate the self as they believe others see them (Cooley, 1902; Mead, 1934).
text.formatted: Their study has foundations in symbolic interactionist theory, which posits that individuals come to evaluate the self as they believe others see them <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Cooley, 1902;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Mead, 1934)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-perceptions also fit within social-cognitive theories of behavior.

In the social information processing model (Crick & Dodge, 1994), meta-perceptions become relevant as youth clarify their goals and assess the likely consequences of different behavioral options (Fontaine et al., 2002; Lansford et al., 2010; Van Dijk et al., 2017), functioning as internalized cognitive guides even when they develop through social learning (Huesmann & Guerra, 1997).
text.formatted: In the social information processing model <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Crick & Dodge, 1994)</ref>, meta-perceptions become relevant as youth clarify their goals and assess the likely consequences of different behavioral options <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Fontaine et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lansford et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Van Dijk et al., 2017)</ref>, functioning as internalized cognitive guides even when they develop through social learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Huesmann & Guerra, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-perceptions inform behavioral decisions across domains ranging from selfpresentation to relationship maintenance (Carlson, 2016).
text.formatted: Meta-perceptions inform behavioral decisions across domains ranging from selfpresentation to relationship maintenance <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Carlson, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analytic evidence suggests that their accuracy is modest at best (Carlson, 2016), though individuals can make valid distinctions between self-perceptions and meta-perceptions (Carlson et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic evidence suggests that their accuracy is modest at best <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Carlson, 2016)</ref>, though individuals can make valid distinctions between self-perceptions and meta-perceptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Carlson et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Inaccuracy may reflect genuine difficulty assessing the private thoughts and evaluations of others (Vazire & Carlson, 2011).
text.formatted: Inaccuracy may reflect genuine difficulty assessing the private thoughts and evaluations of others <ref type="bibr">(Vazire & Carlson, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-accuracy may be especially limited during early adolescence as perspective-taking capacity continues to develop (Choudhury et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Meta-accuracy may be especially limited during early adolescence as perspective-taking capacity continues to develop <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Choudhury et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Early adolescents may struggle more than older adolescents or adults to infer others' evaluations (Harter, 2012).
text.formatted: Early adolescents may struggle more than older adolescents or adults to infer others' evaluations <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Harter, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Fischer's dynamic skills theory, though, suggests that cognitive performance in adolescence is context-dependent and can be scaffolded through task structure (Fischer, 1980; Fischer & Bidell, 2006), such that youth reason more maturely when tasks are concrete and well-supported than when they are abstract and decontextualized (Dawson, 2002; Fischer et al., 1993).
text.formatted: Fischer's dynamic skills theory, though, suggests that cognitive performance in adolescence is context-dependent and can be scaffolded through task structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fischer, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Fischer & Bidell, 2006)</ref>, such that youth reason more maturely when tasks are concrete and well-supported than when they are abstract and decontextualized <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dawson, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Fischer et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Asking early adolescents concrete, specific questions about how friends would react to specific behaviors may therefore scaffold more accurate meta-perceptual judgments despite general constraints on abstract perspective-taking.
Despite their limited accuracy, meta-perceptions may still powerfully influence behavior, as inaccurate beliefs may guide decisions if they feel real to the individual (Carlson & Kenny, 2012).
text.formatted: Despite their limited accuracy, meta-perceptions may still powerfully influence behavior, as inaccurate beliefs may guide decisions if they feel real to the individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Carlson & Kenny, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For middle schoolers, meta-perceptions of friends' evaluations may be particularly influential.
First, friends interact frequently across domains, providing opportunities to communicate approval and disapproval (Laursen & Hartup, 2002).
text.formatted: First, friends interact frequently across domains, providing opportunities to communicate approval and disapproval <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Laursen & Hartup, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Second, friendships during early adolescence involve heightened investment and emotional intensity, which may make perceived approval or disapproval especially salient (Furman & Buhrmester, 1992).
text.formatted: Second, friendships during early adolescence involve heightened investment and emotional intensity, which may make perceived approval or disapproval especially salient <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Furman & Buhrmester, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Third, friends often serve as behavioral models and sources of social comparison, making their evaluative standards salient and known (Prinstein & Dodge, 2008).
text.formatted: Third, friends often serve as behavioral models and sources of social comparison, making their evaluative standards salient and known <ref type="bibr">(Prinstein & Dodge, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The distinction between peer norms and friend-specific meta-perceptions may be particularly important for aggression perpetration among middle schoolers.

Metaperceptions may exert stronger influence on the decision to aggress than general normative beliefs, especially when friends are present, likely to find out about the behavior, or seen as relevant evaluators.
Whether such influence operates between youth or as a process that unfolded within youth over time has not been established.
Understanding how expectations about friends' reactions related to aggression requires distinguishing two questions.
The social-cognitive account described above is a within-person process, but youth also differ from one another in relatively stable ways (e.g., the friendships they form).

Most evidence linking norms and normative beliefs to aggression comes from cross-sectional data, two-way designs (e.g., Huesmann & Guerra, 1997), or cross-lagged models that do not partition more stable between-person variance from within-person change (e.g., Krahé & Busching, 2014).
text.formatted: Most evidence linking norms and normative beliefs to aggression comes from cross-sectional data, two-way designs (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Huesmann & Guerra, 1997)</ref>, or cross-lagged models that do not partition more stable between-person variance from within-person change (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Krahé & Busching, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Cross-lagged estimates from such models can reflect stable individual differences and misrepresent prospective processes (Hamaker et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Cross-lagged estimates from such models can reflect stable individual differences and misrepresent prospective processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hamaker et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work on perceived peer norms and aggression has explicitly called for random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs; Bullo & Schulz, 2025).
text.formatted: Recent work on perceived peer norms and aggression has explicitly called for random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs; <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bullo & Schulz, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, the between-person and withinperson associations between expected friend reactions and aggression perpetration have not been examined separately; clarifying which level carries these associations is a central contribution of the present study.

To that end, we examined the longitudinal associations between meta-perceptions of aggressive and nonaggressive behaviors and reported physical and relational aggression perpetration among early adolescents.
Overall, we expected the social cognitive meta-perceptions of aggressive and non-aggressive behaviors to inform their reported aggression perpetration.
We pre-registered several hypotheses (https://osf.io/q27a9/overview?view_only=5c1dd775967744f8bcbadaf51efc7a6a ).
text.formatted: We pre-registered several hypotheses (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/q27a9/overview?view_only=5c1dd775967744f8bcbadaf51efc7a6a">https://osf.io/q27a9/overview?view_only=5c1dd775967744f8bcbadaf51efc7a6a</ref> ).

text.text: At the between-person level, we hypothesized that youth who generally expect their friends to be supportive of aggressive behavior will report greater physical aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 3) and relational aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 6).

Additionally, we hypothesized that youth who generally expect their friends to be more supportive of nonviolent behaviors would report lower physical aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 9) and relational aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 12).
At the within-person level, we expected meta-perceptions and aggression to be dynamically linked across waves, consistent with the social-cognitive account of response evaluation.

Regarding meta-perceptions of aggressive behaviors, we hypothesized that, within-participants, relatively greater expectation for friends' support for aggressive behaviors at one timepoint will predict relatively greater physical aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 1) and relational aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 4) at the subsequent timepoint, and that relatively greater physical aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 2) and relational aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 5) will predict relatively greater expectations for friends' support for aggressive behaviors at the subsequent timepoint.

Regarding meta-perceptions of nonviolent behaviors, we hypothesized that, within-participants, relatively greater expectation for friends' support for nonviolent behavior at one timepoint will predict relatively lower physical aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 7) and relational aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 10) at the subsequent timepoint, and that relatively lower physical aggression perpetration (Hypothesis 8) and relational aggression perpetuation (Hypothesis 11) will predict relatively greater expectations for friends' support for nonviolent behaviors at the subsequent timepoint.

text.text: We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
These analyses represent secondary data analyses of data from a project designed to evaluate the impact of a school-based violence prevention curriculum (see Sullivan et al., 2015).
text.formatted: These analyses represent secondary data analyses of data from a project designed to evaluate the impact of a school-based violence prevention curriculum (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Sullivan et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were sixth and seventh grade students enrolled in one of three middle schools in and around a medium-sized city in the Southeastern United States.
Two of these schools were situated in an urban setting; the third school was a semi-rural school in an adjoining county.

All students at the schools were eligible to participate if they were enrolled in the sixth grade during the 2008-2009 school year, enrolled in the seventh grade during the 2009-2010 school year, and were not in selfcontained homeroom classes.
The urban schools served a predominately Black student population while the semi-rural (i.e., "Rural Fringe" by the Census Bureau) served a more diverse student population.
For the purposes of these analyses, we retained participants who completed at least two surveys.
In total, 527 students completed at least two surveys.
On average, participants were 11.32 years old (SD = 0.63, Missing: 8) at the time of the first survey.
Across the study period, 520 participants completed the full battery of questionnaires at Timepoint 1, 474 at Timepoint 2, 428 at Timepoint 3, and 406 at Timepoint 4.
Much of the attrition can be attributed to participants moving away from the study's school sites (Sullivan et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Much of the attrition can be attributed to participants moving away from the study's school sites <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Sullivan et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Disparities in missing data at each timepoint may be influenced by the questionnaire's location in the full battery or a participant's decision to skip a measure.
Sociodemographic information about the participants from each school may be found in Table 1.
text.formatted: Sociodemographic information about the participants from each school may be found in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Using archival data from the state's Department of Education, the proportions of ethnoracial identity and gender in the samples approximate the proportions of the full student body (Virginia Department of Education, 2010).
text.formatted: Using archival data from the state's Department of Education, the proportions of ethnoracial identity and gender in the samples approximate the proportions of the full student body <ref type="bibr">(Virginia Department of Education, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Students were recruited as part of the larger efforts of the project.
Students in all non-self-contained homeroom classes were approached either individually or in small groups to introduce the project and review assent and consent forms.
The potential participants and their parents received a copy of the consent form.

Potential participants received a $5 USD Walmart gift card for showing the form to their parents and returning it to the research staff, regardless of whether parental consent to participate was provided.
When parental consent and student assent were obtained, participants were scheduled to complete the assessment at the participating middle schools.
Parental consent and student assent were obtained from 83% of the eligible students from the urban schools and 75% of the eligible students from the rural fringe school (Bettencourt et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Parental consent and student assent were obtained from 83% of the eligible students from the urban schools and 75% of the eligible students from the rural fringe school <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bettencourt et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were compensated with a $10 USD Walmart gift card for their participation in the survey.
Note.
We were missing data from seven participants.
Self-report measures were completed by participants at four timepoints (i.e., the beginning and end of the school year for sixth and seventh grade).
The surveys were completed using a Computer Aided Self-Interviewing (CASI) modality.
Questions were displayed virtually on the computer screen while participants listened to audio recording of each question through headphones to compensate for reading difficulties.

Participants responded to questions independently, but research assistants were available to aid participants who had questions or experienced difficulties with completing the full battery of questionnaires.
Additionally, the research assistants read instructions regarding the purpose of the testing, confidentiality, and the right not to participate.
Meta-perceptions of friends' reactions were measured using the Friends'
Reaction to Responses to Conflict Situations Scale (Farrell et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Reaction to Responses to Conflict Situations Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Farrell et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were instructed that these questions referred to the participant and their friends, as compared to the broader peer network in classrooms.
The measure included six hypothetical, but likely, scenarios that describe a challenging situation that might arise (e.g., "You and another kid get into an argument at school.

Other students are there boosting it up saying, 'Fight, fight, fight.'") and asked to "think of how your friends might react if you tried the different ways of dealing with these difficult situations".

All scenarios were followed by two questions that asked about meta-perceptions of their friends' reactions if they enacted an aggressive behavior (e.g., "What would your friends think if you threw the first punch?") or non-violent behavior (e.g., What would your friends think if you tried to talk to the person calmly to settle the argument?).
The full measure may be found in the Supplemental Materials.
For each behavior, participants selected whether they thought their friends would support (scored as 1), not support (scored as -1), or be neutral (scored as 0) about each behavior.

As such, six questions (i.e., one question per scenario) measured meta-perceptions about friends' support for aggressive behaviors and six questions measured meta-perceptions about friends' support for non-violent behaviors.

Most importantly, these questions probed contextualized and concrete behaviors which may support the scaffolding necessary for early adolescents to engage in accurate meta-perceptual judgements (Fischer, 1980; Fischer & Bidell, 2006).
text.formatted: Most importantly, these questions probed contextualized and concrete behaviors which may support the scaffolding necessary for early adolescents to engage in accurate meta-perceptual judgements <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fischer, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Fischer & Bidell, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Physical and relational aggression perpetration were measured using the Problem Behaviors Frequency Scale -Revised (PBFS-R; Farrell et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Physical and relational aggression perpetration were measured using the Problem Behaviors Frequency Scale -Revised (PBFS-R; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Farrell et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Participants reported how frequently they enacted specific behaviors in the past 30 days using a 6-point anchored scale (1 = Never,2 = 1-2 times,3 = 3-5 times,4 = 6-9 times,5 = 10-19 times,6 = 20 or more times).
Each item included a decline to answer option.
For the present study, we used only the items which were available in the dataset and identified in prior psychometric work of the PBFS (Farrell et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For the present study, we used only the items which were available in the dataset and identified in prior psychometric work of the PBFS <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Farrell et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Physical aggression perpetration was assessed with five items (e.g., "Hit or slapped someone", "Thrown something at someone to hurt them").
Relational aggression was assessed with six items (e.g., "Spread a false rumor about someone", "Made fun of someone to make others laugh").
Prior to our hypothesis tests, we calculated the mean for all variables at each time point.
Then, we conducted two separate RI-CLPMs.
Variance inflation factors indicated no evidence of problematic multicollinearity among peer reactions to nonviolence and aggression (all VIFs < 2.0).
text.formatted: Variance inflation factors indicated no evidence of problematic multicollinearity among peer reactions to nonviolence and aggression (all VIFs < 2.0).

text.text: As such, we report combined models with expectations of friend reactions to both positive and negative behaviors as independent predictors.
We specified separate models for each outcome variable (i.e., physical and relational aggression perpetration).
Our two-model approach was guided by two considerations.

First, a single model incorporating cross-lagged and random-intercept parameters, along with their covariance, would have substantially increased model complexity relative to our sample size, raising concerns about power to detect the within-person effects central to our hypotheses.

Second, we reasoned that statistically controlling for the overlap between physical and relational aggression risked producing residualized effects that would be difficult to interpret across the broader literature, which typically treats these as related but distinct forms of aggression.
Within each model, we constrained autoregressive and cross-lagged paths to be equal across time.
All models were estimated using full information maximum likelihood to account for missing data at each timepoint.
For each model, we dummy coded intervention condition and school site and regressed these variables onto random intercepts to control for context-specific influences on reported aggressive behaviors.
We fixed observed residual variances to 0, so all variance was partitioned into stable betweenand-within person variances.

In line with our pre-registered analysis plan, we attempted to conduct a sensitivity power analysis using the powRICLPM package for R (Mulder, 2023) to identify the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) with 80% power for the cross-lagged effects and the random intercept correlations (see Giner-Sorolla et al., 2024).

text.text: Unfortunately, due to the mathematical constraints which arose from the models' high intraclass correlations and moderate random intercept correlations, formal MDES calculations using this package were not feasible.

These constraints reflect the mathematical incompatibility between high between-person variance and the additional complexity of cross-lagged parameters, resulting in non-positive definite covariance matrices in the power simulation framework.
This is a limitation of the package's utility for sensitivity power analysis.
It is unclear if null results for within-person effects are due to a lack of power or the absence of a true effect.
With that in mind, all conclusions regarding within-person cross-lagged effects should be viewed cautiously until an agreed-upon process for conducting sensitivity analyses for RI-CLPMs emerges.
The effect sizes reported here can be used to guide future a priori power analyses, an area where the powRICLPM package demonstrates excellent utility.

Regarding the between-person associations between random intercepts, a sensitivity analysis using the pwr package for R (Champely, 2020) indicated we can detect correlations as small as |r| = 0.18 with 90% power at = .05 with 𝛼 N = 304 (i.e., the smallest number of cases for any variable across all waves).

text.text: Overall, our inferences remain unchanged.

The present study examined whether early adolescents' meta-perceptions about friends' reactions to aggressive and non-violent conflict resolution strategies prospectively predict physical and relational aggression perpetration.
Using RI-CLPMs across four timepoints, we found statistically significant between-person associations.

Youth who generally believed their friends supported aggressive responses to conflict situations tended to engage in more physical and relational aggression, whereas those who believed their friends supported non-violent responses tended to engage in less.
Perceived friend support for aggressive and non-violent responses thus functioned as promotive and constraining factors, respectively.

The only statistically significant withinperson effect indicated that relational aggression perpetration predicted higher perceived support for aggressive conflict resolution strategies at the subsequent timepoint.

The statistically significant associations between random intercepts indicate substantial between-person covariation, consistent with previous research linking perceived peer norms to involvement in aggressive behavior (e.g., Henry et al., 2000; Salmivalli & Voeten, 2004).
text.formatted: The statistically significant associations between random intercepts indicate substantial between-person covariation, consistent with previous research linking perceived peer norms to involvement in aggressive behavior (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Henry et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Salmivalli & Voeten, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of statistically significant cross-lagged paths indicates that this covariation does not reflect within-person change processes operating across the study period.
The lack of widespread convergence between between-person and within-person effects carries important theoretical implications (Hamaker et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The lack of widespread convergence between between-person and within-person effects carries important theoretical implications <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hamaker et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Traditional cross-lagged panel models, which do not partition variance into these components, can yield misleading cross-lagged coefficients when constructs show stable between-person associations, because apparent prospective effects may reflect stable third variables.
The RI-CLPM's separation of stable and time-varying components provides a more rigorous test of whether one variable predicts changes in the other.
An additional, non-mutually exclusive possibility concerns developmental timing.
Because early adolescence is when friends emerge as salient social referents, friendspecific meta-perceptual schemas may still have been consolidating among participants.

Between-person differences may already reflect meaningfully different schemas rooted in youth's friendship histories, while the schemas may not yet fluctuate enough to produce detectable within-person cross-lagged effects.

Assessing the construct across a wider developmental period, spanning the increasingly strong role of peer social orientation in early adolescence, would clarify whether within-person dynamics strengthen as schemas mature or are more detectable earlier, before schemas stabilize around established friendship configurations.

Statistically significant between-person associations without widespread crosslagged effects may suggest that selection processes play an important role in the observed covariation, an alternative explanation deserving of focused inquiry.
Youth with higher levels of aggressive behavior may select friends who hold pro-aggressive attitudes or may selectively attend to and remember instances when friends condoned aggressive responses.
This idea may be supported by the statistically significant crosslagged effect of relational aggression perpetration on expected reactions to aggressive conflict situation responses.
Friend similarity reflects selection as much as or more than mutual influence (e.g., Kandel, 1978; Prinstein & Dodge, 2008).
text.formatted: Friend similarity reflects selection as much as or more than mutual influence (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kandel, 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Prinstein & Dodge, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Social network analyses show that homophily (i.e., the tendency to form friendships with similar others) accounts for substantial friendship similarity in aggressive behaviors (Sijtsema et al., 2010; Veenstra et al., 2013), as youth preferentially select friends who are behaviorally and attitudinally similar to themselves (McPherson et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Social network analyses show that homophily (i.e., the tendency to form friendships with similar others) accounts for substantial friendship similarity in aggressive behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Sijtsema et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Veenstra et al., 2013)</ref>, as youth preferentially select friends who are behaviorally and attitudinally similar to themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(McPherson et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal network analyses further suggest that selection processes may be particularly prominent during early adolescence (Logis et al., 2013; Molano et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Longitudinal network analyses further suggest that selection processes may be particularly prominent during early adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Logis et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Molano et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive consistency processes could also maintain stable perceptions of friends' responses, leading youth to hold meta-perceptions that align with their behavioral tendencies even without accurate information about friends' actual attitudes.

Youth who behave aggressively may engage in biased information processing that leads them to perceive friends as more supportive of aggression than they actually are, whereas youth who aggress less may consistently interpret friends as more supportive of non-violent behaviors.
Such biases would create more stable between-person covariation without meta-perceptions causally influencing behavior.

Shared third variables (e.g., neighborhood contexts, family socialization practices, individual personality traits) could also influence both aggressive behavior (e.g., as protection from environmental harm) and meta-perceptions.
The absence of widespread meta-perception effects on aggression should not be interpreted as evidence against peer influence more broadly.

Peer contexts are vastly important throughout adolescence (Slagter et al., 2023; Prinstein & Dodge, 2008; Zingora & Flache, 2025), and the mechanisms linking them to aggressive behavior may differ from those examined in the present study.
text.formatted: Peer contexts are vastly important throughout adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Slagter et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Prinstein & Dodge, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Zingora & Flache, 2025)</ref>, and the mechanisms linking them to aggressive behavior may differ from those examined in the present study.

text.text: Direct and immediate social reinforcement may matter more than cognitive expectancies about generalized approval.

Friends may laugh at an aggressive act, show fear, or increase their evaluations of a perpetrator's social status in the moment, and such consequences may shape behavior more powerfully than abstract beliefs about whether friends generally approve of aggressive or nonviolent responses to conflict situations.
Behavioral modeling represents another mechanism that does not require meta-perceptions.

Youth may imitate friends' aggressive behaviors through social learning processes (i.e., Bandura, 1973), particularly when aggression appears to be a successful means of achieving a desired end-state, making friends' actual aggressive behavior a more proximal influence on youth aggression than youth's metaperceptions.
text.formatted: Youth may imitate friends' aggressive behaviors through social learning processes (i.e., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bandura, 1973)</ref>, particularly when aggression appears to be a successful means of achieving a desired end-state, making friends' actual aggressive behavior a more proximal influence on youth aggression than youth's metaperceptions.

text.text: Peer influence could also operate through identity processes and selfcategorization, which do not depend on outcome expectancies.

Early adolescents may adopt behavioral characteristics of their social network to affirm their membership and express their social identity (e.g., Tarrant et al., 2006), a process involving perceived behavioral norms that define group membership.
text.formatted: Early adolescents may adopt behavioral characteristics of their social network to affirm their membership and express their social identity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Tarrant et al., 2006)</ref>, a process involving perceived behavioral norms that define group membership.

text.text: Several limitations warrant discussion.

First, data were collected between 2008 and 2010, and evidence is mixed regarding technology's impact on adolescents' abstract thinking and capacity for meta-perceptions (e.g., Adelantado-Renau et al., 2019), so the findings may not generalize to contemporary early adolescents.
text.formatted: First, data were collected between 2008 and 2010, and evidence is mixed regarding technology's impact on adolescents' abstract thinking and capacity for meta-perceptions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Adelantado-Renau et al., 2019)</ref>, so the findings may not generalize to contemporary early adolescents.

text.text: Second, while the sociodemographic diversity and inclusion of students in both urban and rural areas is a strength of the study, we did not delve into subgroup analyses.
We are unable to make claims about any one subgroup of participants.
Future research could investigate the role of ethnoracial identity, socialization practices, and context between rural and urban areas.

Third, aggression was self-reported and may have been misremembered or misreported; future research might utilize objective measures of aggressive behavior (e.g., Taylor Aggression Paradigm; Taylor, 1967).
text.formatted: Third, aggression was self-reported and may have been misremembered or misreported; future research might utilize objective measures of aggressive behavior (e.g., Taylor Aggression Paradigm; <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Taylor, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: Ultimately, the findings underscore the value of distinguishing selection from influence processes.
Future research might examine meta-perceptions at multiple temporal resolutions.

Moderately intensive timescales (e.g., daily, weekly) could test whether situation-specific meta-perceptions predict proximal aggressive or non-violent responses, whereas longer intervals might detect cumulative effects not apparent across a semester-based period.
Network analyses might identify which network members influence meta-perceptions, aggressive behavior perpetration, or both.

Future research should also examine alternative mechanisms, including direct reinforcement, behavioral modeling, identity processes, and structural features of peer networks, that might operate independently or interactively with meta-perceptual processes.

Youth who generally perceived their friends as supportive of aggressive responses to conflict situations reported higher frequencies of relational and physical aggression, and those who perceived their friends as supportive of non-violent responses reported lower frequencies; the only within-person prospective effect ran from relational aggression perpetration to expected reactions to aggressive responses.
Distinguishing individual differences from dynamic change processes is therefore essential for assessing associations between meta-perceptions and aggressive behavior during early adolescence.

text.text: This next set of questions is about you and your friends.
Here we describe some difficult situations and some different ways of handling them.
For each question, think of how your friends might react if you tried the different ways of dealing with these difficult situations.
Imagine that you're in the following situation: SITUATION 1: You see two kids your age about ready to start a fight in school. 1a.
What would your friends think if you cheered on the fight ?
1 They would think that I was trill.
2 They would think I should have stayed out of it.
3 They would not care.
4 Skip 1b.
What would your friends think if you went to get a teacher ?
1 They would think I was being a snitch.
2 They would not care.
3 They would think I did the right thing.
4 Skip Now imagine that you're in the following situation: SITUATION 2: You and your friends are playing ball on the playground.
Another kid your age who's watching the game keeps making fun of the way you are playing. 2a.
What would your friends think if you started a fight with the kid who was making fun of you?
1 They would think I was tough.
2 They would not care.
3 They would think I did the wrong thing.
4 Skip 2b.
What would your friends think if you quit playing ball and left ?
1 They would think I was being a punk.
2 They would think I'm ok.
3 They would not care.
4 Skip Now imagine that you're in the following situation: SITUATION 3: You and another kid get into an argument at school.
Other students are there boosting it up saying, "Fight, fight, fight." 3a.
What would your friends think if you tried to talk to the person calmly to settle the argument?
1 They would think I was a wimp.
2 They would not care.
3 They would think I was smart.
4 Skip 3b.
What would your friends think if you threw the first punch ?
1 They would think that I'm cool.
2 They would think I was whack.
3 They would not care.
4 Skip Now imagine that you're in the following situation: SITUATION 4: Somebody is spreading a rumor about a student and you got blamed for it.
Now you have a big problem with the person who thinks you were talking about them behind their back. 4a.
What would your friends think if you talked it out with the person the rumor was started about and explained that you didn't start it ?
1 They would think that I did the right thing.
2 They would think I was weak.
3 They would not care.
4 Skip 4b.
What would your friends think if you argued and got into a fight with the person who blamed you for starting the rumor ?
1 They would think that I'm tough.
2 They would think I was being dumb.
3 They would not care.
4 Skip Now imagine that you're in the following situation: SITUATION 5: Another kid at school says something to you that is disrespectful about your family. 5a.
What would your friends think if you gave the other kid a serious look and told them if they didn't stop, there would be trouble ?
1 They would think that I did the right thing.
2 They would think I was whack.
3 They would not care.
4 Skip 5b.
What would your friends think if you you just ignored them and didn't let it bother you ?
1 They would think that I'm cool.
2 They would think I was being dumb.
3 They would not care.
4 Skip Now imagine that you're in the following situation: SITUATION 6: There's a group of kids at school that tease and pick on you.
They call you names and make fun of you. 6a.
What would your friends think if you asked an adult at school, like a teacher or principal, for help ?
1 They would think that I did the right thing.
2 They would think I was a punk.
3 They would not care.
4 Skip 6b.
What would your friends think if you asked them to help you beat up the other kids ?
1 They would think that I'm trill.
2 They would think it was a bad idea.
3 They would not care.
